Hook: Ricursive's Ripple-65B Preview leads, with a $32M training-cost claim and a company-reported benchmark lead.

Story 1
Headline: Ricursive releases Ripple-65B Preview, an open-weight model it says cost $32M to develop
Card: Ricursive's Ripple-65B Preview: open weights, $32M claimed R&D cost
Narration: Ricursive says its new open-weight model, Ripple-65B Preview, scored eighty point five two on TerminalBench two point one. The company says it spent thirty-two million dollars on full research and development. Those results have not been independently verified.
Summary: Ricursive Intelligence released Ripple-65B Preview on November 12, a general-purpose variant of the proprietary model behind its AI chip design platform. Ricursive says the dense Transformer was pretrained on 12 trillion tokens, supports up to 1M context, and is available on Hugging Face, Together AI, GMI Cloud, OpenRouter and Fireworks. The company says the model scored 80.52 on TerminalBench 2.1, ahead of several open-weight rivals, and that its full R&D cost was $32M.
Why it matters: Developers choosing open-weight models for coding agents may weigh Ricursive's claimed low training cost and its claim that the model runs on local hardware such as NVIDIA DGX Spark.

Story 2
Headline: ReTrace turns agent runs into workflows where code, not an LLM, picks each step
Card: ReTrace: coded workflows replace LLM step-picking, at 24% lower cost per task
Narration: Researchers present ReTrace, which turns agent runs into workflows where code, not a language model, chooses each step. The authors say it cuts cost per task by twenty-four percent, though it trails the agent slightly on accuracy.
Summary: Researchers present ReTrace, a method that turns a standard operating procedure and a few logged agent runs into a reusable workflow. The authors say LLM agents call a model to choose every step, which adds latency and cost at scale, and ReTrace lets code select the next step instead. In their reported tests on 79 procedures, ReTrace workflows reached 93.8% completion versus 96.8% for the agent, at 24% lower cost per task.
Why it matters: Teams running many automated business procedures could cut cost per task and latency if coded workflows keep most of an agent's accuracy.

Story 3
Headline: LeRobot v0.7.0 adds streamed-data training and interactive robot control
Card: LeRobot v0.7.0: train on streamed data, steer robots from the terminal
Narration: Hugging Face says LeRobot version zero point seven lets robotics developers train on streamed datasets without downloading them first. It also adds interactive control, so users can steer a running robot from the terminal.
Summary: Hugging Face says LeRobot v0.7.0 lets users train on datasets streamed from the Hub, a Storage Bucket or LanceDB without downloading them first. The release also adds interactive rollouts for switching subtasks and steering a running robot from the terminal, plus four world action models and four new VLA models. The Hub now hosts almost 300 TB of open physical AI data in LeRobot format.
Why it matters: Robotics developers can train on large open datasets without local copies, and run policies on a remote GPU while the robot's own computer handles cameras and motors.

Story 4
Headline: NVIDIA, Rebellions and SK Telecom partner on Korean sovereign AI infrastructure
Card: NVIDIA, Rebellions and SK Telecom: NPUs and GPUs for Korean sovereign AI
Narration: NVIDIA says its NVLink Fusion technology will connect Korean chipmaker Rebellions' R200 processors to its platform. SK Telecom plans to deploy the systems in its AI data center. The R200 systems are expected to be ready in twenty twenty-eight.
Summary: NVIDIA, Rebellions and SK Telecom announced a collaboration to advance Korea's sovereign AI infrastructure using NVIDIA NVLink Fusion. NVIDIA says the technology lets chipmakers combine specialized silicon with its scale-up networking, and Rebellions will connect its Rebel R200 NPUs to the NVIDIA platform using the MGX rack architecture. SK Telecom plans to deploy the systems in its AI data center, and the companies plan disaggregated inference with NVIDIA GPUs for prefill and Rebellions NPUs for decode.
Why it matters: Korean operators such as SK Telecom would deploy these systems, expanding domestic options for AI infrastructure built with local NPU chips alongside NVIDIA hardware.

Story 5
Headline: UK sovereign AI fund and British Business Bank back chip startup Fractile
Card: UK backs Fractile, valued at over £5 billion in a £500 million-plus round
Narration: The UK government and the British Business Bank have backed Fractile, a London and Bristol AI chip startup. The government says the round values the company at over five billion pounds.
Summary: The UK Government's Sovereign AI Venture Fund and the British Business Bank have backed Fractile, a London and Bristol-based AI chip startup, in a Series C round worth over £500 million. The government says the round values Fractile at over £5 billion and that the company is rebuilding AI hardware to be faster, more energy efficient and less costly. Investors include CapitalG, Lightspeed and Redpoint, and the government's individual investment amounts are not disclosed.
Why it matters: The government says the investment could reduce reliance on overseas technology for UK companies that depend on AI hardware.

Story 2
Headline: ReTrace turns agent runs into workflows where code, not an LLM, picks each step
Card: ReTrace: workflows run in 1.3s vs 170s for the agent (authors' results)
Narration: The authors report ReTrace, which turns a procedure and a few logged runs into a workflow where code picks each step. On tau-squared Bench it runs in one point three seconds versus one hundred seventy for the agent.
Summary: The authors present ReTrace, a method that turns a procedure document and a few logged agent runs into a reusable workflow. The authors report 93.8% completion versus 96.8% for the agent on 79 production procedures, at 24% lower cost per task. On τ²-Bench they report 75.8% success versus 80.6%, and a run time of 1.3 seconds instead of 170.

Hugging Face says GPU image augmentation makes ACT train 2.8x faster on an H100 and 3.3x faster on an A100.
Why it matters: Robotics developers can train on the Hub's almost 300 TB of open Physical AI data without downloading it, and run models on a remote GPU workstation while the robot handles its own hardware.

Summary: Anthropic says Claude Fable 5.2 and Claude Mythos 5.2 are the same underlying model. Fable has cybersecurity and biology safeguards that let it be offered to all users. Mythos access requires applying through verification programs.
Why it matters: Users choosing between the two names should know they run the same model, and that access depends on which version they can obtain.

Story 2
Headline: Dr. RTL: a multi-agent framework for autonomous chip design optimization
Card: Dr. RTL: AI agents that optimize chip design code
Narration: Researchers report that Dr. RTL, a multi-agent framework, improves chip designs across twenty real-world tests. The authors report twenty-one percent better timing and six percent less area than commercial synthesis. These results are not independently verified.
Summary: Researchers Wenji Fang, Yao Lu, Jinghua Wang and Zhiyao Xie present Dr. RTL, a multi-agent framework that automates critical-path analysis, RTL rewriting and implementation-level evaluation. The authors say it continuously improves through reusable optimization skills. The authors report average timing improvements of 21% and 17% with a 6% area reduction over commercial synthesis on 20 real-world RTL designs. The paper was submitted to arXiv on November 10, 2026.
Why it matters: Chip design engineers and electronic design automation teams are affected, because the work explores agents that rewrite RTL code and tune synthesis scripts.

Story 3
Headline: PyTorch 2.15 makes the new NCCL backend default and adds Apple Silicon updates
Card: PyTorch 2.15: new default NCCL backend and Apple Silicon updates
Narration: PyTorch 2.15 was released on October twenty-eighth. PyTorch says its rewritten NCCL backend is now the default for distributed training. Python three point ten support has been dropped. Apple Silicon gets new float8 support.
Summary: PyTorch 2.15 was released on October 28, 2026, with 3,117 commits from 583 contributors since PyTorch 2.14. PyTorch says its rewritten NCCL backend is now the default for every NCCL process group, with rollback options. The release also adds a flight recorder for hangs, a one-sided transfer API marked unstable, and float8 support on Apple Silicon. PyTorch 2.15 drops Python 3.10 and macOS 14 support for MPS.
Why it matters: Developers running distributed PyTorch training and Apple Silicon users are affected, and must move to Python 3.11 or newer and macOS 15 or newer for MPS.

Story 4
Headline: Anthropic expands GSA partnership with a 40% discount for government buyers
Card: GSA deal: 40% discount on Claude for government buyers
Narration: Anthropic says a new agreement with GSA gives government partners a forty percent discount on Claude. The discount reaches state, local, tribal and territorial governments. Anthropic estimates it will save the government one billion dollars.
Summary: Anthropic says a new agreement with GSA gives government partners a 40% discount on Claude Enterprise, Claude for Government and the Claude API. The discount extends to state, local, tribal and territorial governments. Anthropic says about 500 US federal, state and local organizations now use Claude, and estimates the discounts will save the government $1 billion.
Why it matters: Government agencies buying Claude can get the discount and pay only for the usage they consume, since no minimum spend is required.

Story 5
Headline: NIST publishes ten voluntary practices for super intelligence incident response
Card: Ten voluntary practices for super intelligence incident response
Narration: NIST, with partners at the NSA and CISA, published ten voluntary practices for managing incidents in super intelligence training. The practices cover five stages, from preparation through reporting. Further work is planned for future phases.
Summary: NIST CAISSI, the NSA's Super Intelligence Security Center and CISA published ten key practices on October 16, 2026, for managing incidents during super intelligence training and evaluation. The document is voluntary and focuses on cases where agents take significant uninstructed actions that break operator-set controls. The ten practices cover five stages: preparation, detection, response, recovery and reporting.
Why it matters: Frontier AI developers running super intelligence training and evaluations are the audience, since the guidance helps them prepare for, detect and report incidents.
